prompt: The staging token in `ci/dast.sh` and the signing password in `~/ci/keys` are both secrets the pipeline uses. Why is the staging token the smaller worry?

choices.text: It is shorter, so it is harder to guess
choices.why: Eighteen random bytes cannot be guessed either way. The difference is how long each one keeps working.

choices.text: It lives for one run and dies with its container
choices.why: Right. A leaked copy unlocks a staging service that no longer exists.

choices.text: It is base64, which keeps it out of a readable log
choices.why: base64 is an encoding. Anybody reading the log can decode it in one command.

choices.text: Only the DAST stage reads it
choices.why: The password is also read by one stage only, `sign`. Which stage reads a secret is not what separates the two.

prompt: `~/ci/keys/password` is mode 600 and belongs to `ana`. Which runs of linkbox's pipeline can read it?

choices.text: Only runs of `main`, the branch that signs releases
choices.why: Nothing in the hook looks at the branch before running the pipeline.

choices.text: None: mode 600 keeps the file away from processes
choices.why: Mode 600 lets its owner read it, and every pipeline runs as its owner.

choices.text: Every run of every branch
choices.why: Right. The hook runs each pushed branch's pipeline as `ana`, and the branch's own `ci/` decides what the run does.

choices.text: Only runs whose earlier stages all passed
choices.why: Any stage of the run can read a file `ana` can read; a branch can change the first one.

prompt: Every secrets manager needs a first credential that unlocks it, and keeping that credential somewhere is called the secret ___ problem.
Which of these is a dev-mode convenience that a production Vault turns into a control?

choices.text: Answering requests on port 8200
choices.why: A production Vault listens on 8200 too. The port is not what changes.

choices.text: Keeping secrets under paths such as `secret/`
choices.why: Paths and the key/value store work the same in production.

choices.text: Accepting tokens in an HTTP header
choices.why: Every Vault takes its token that way; production adds TLS around it.

choices.text: Starting unsealed
choices.why: Right. A production Vault starts sealed and cannot read its own storage until it is unsealed.

prompt: A policy grants `read` on `secret/linkbox/signing`, the path used with `vault kv put`, and the pipeline's read of that secret is refused. Why?

choices.text: The policy needs `list` as well as `read`
choices.why: `list` shows names under a path. Reading one known path needs only `read`, on the right path.

choices.text: Version 2 of the store puts `data/` in the path
choices.why: Right. The API path is `secret/data/linkbox/signing`, and policies match API paths, not the CLI's shorter one.

choices.text: Policies take effect only after the server restarts
choices.why: A policy applies to the next request. Restarting a dev server would lose everything.

choices.text: A dev server ignores policies for HTTP requests
choices.why: Dev mode enforces policies exactly as production does; the lesson's denials came from it.

prompt: Why does every `vault` command in the lesson act with root's power?

choices.text: `VAULT_ADDR` points at 127.0.0.1
choices.why: The address says where the server is, not who is asking.

choices.text: The client runs inside the container, where dev mode left the root token
choices.why: Right. That is the operator's tool; the pipeline uses `curl` and its own token.

choices.text: Membership of the `docker` group is equivalent to root
choices.why: True of the machine, as lesson 16 said, but Vault decides by the token, not by the Unix user.

choices.text: The image runs its server as the Unix user root
choices.why: Vault's permissions have nothing to do with the operating system's users.

prompt: With the `linkbox-sign` token, a read of `secret/data/linkbox/registry` answers "permission denied" and never "not found". Why does Vault not say whether that path exists?

choices.text: It would let a token map what it is refused
choices.why: Right. Telling a missing path from a forbidden one would reveal what exists beyond the policy.

choices.text: Because the path does not exist, and Vault reports that as a denial
choices.why: It answers the same whether the path exists or not; that is the point.

choices.text: HTTP has no status code for a missing secret
choices.why: HTTP has 404, and Vault uses it where the token may read the path.

choices.text: Dev mode hides the reason for every error
choices.why: The expired token's error gave two reasons; dev mode hides nothing.

prompt: Thirty seconds after it was made, the hand-made token's read answers "permission denied" and "invalid token". Who revoked it?

choices.text: The `trap` in the pipeline's script
choices.why: That `trap` belongs to `ci/vault-read.sh`, and this token never went near it.

choices.text: The root token, on a schedule Vault keeps
choices.why: No schedule and no root action were involved.

choices.text: Nobody: its time to live ran out, and Vault forgot it
choices.why: Right. Expiry needs no action from anybody, which is its whole value.

choices.text: The `default` policy, which every token carries
choices.why: `default` lets a token revoke itself; it does not do it on its own.

prompt: A team gives its pipeline `read` on `secret/data/payments/*` "to keep things simple". What is wrong with it?

choices.text: Vault refuses wildcards in policy paths
choices.why: A trailing `*` is valid, which is why it is so easy to write.

choices.text: It reaches secrets added there later
choices.why: Right. Every secret anybody stores under that prefix later is granted too, without anyone deciding it.

choices.text: It also grants `update` on those paths
choices.why: Capabilities are listed one by one; `read` grants reading and nothing else.

choices.text: It removes the token's time to live
choices.why: A policy says what may be done, not for how long.

prompt: Anybody who copies an identity token out of a log can decode and read its claims. Why is that acceptable?

choices.text: The claims are encrypted with the CI server's key
choices.why: They are base64url, an encoding; `jq` decoded them in the lesson.

choices.text: Only Vault knows how to decode base64url
choices.why: Any tool decodes it, as the lesson's one `jq` command did.

choices.text: No secret is in them; a signature vouches
choices.why: Right. Reading them gains nothing; changing them breaks the signature.

choices.text: The claims are hashed and cannot be read back
choices.why: Only the signature is computed over them; the claims themselves are plain JSON.

prompt: In the token `mint.py` made for `main`, how many seconds separate `iat` from `exp`?
What happens to the secret zero problem once the CI server signs identity tokens?

choices.text: No long-lived secret is left anywhere
choices.why: The private key is long-lived; it simply never reaches a run.

choices.text: The private key moves into Vault with the password
choices.why: Vault holds the public key. The private key stays with the CI server.

choices.text: One remains, the private key, and no run holds it
choices.why: Right. A run holds a token the key signed, which dies in five minutes.

choices.text: Each run gets a private key of its own
choices.why: Runs get signed tokens, not keys; one key signs them all.

prompt: Somebody edits the `ref` claim of a `try-something` token to `refs/heads/main`, keeps the rest, and sends it to Vault's `linkbox-main` role. What happens?

choices.text: Refused: the signature no longer matches the claims
choices.why: Right. The signature covers the claims byte for byte, so the edit breaks it.

choices.text: It is accepted, since the claims now match the role exactly
choices.why: The claims match, but they are no longer the ones the CI server signed.

choices.text: It is accepted for five minutes and then revoked
choices.why: It never gets a Vault token to revoke.

choices.text: It is refused because its `jti` was used already
choices.why: Vault accepted one token twice in the lesson; it does not track `jti` here.

prompt: The role `linkbox-any` checked only the audience. Why did a run of `try-something` get the signing policy through it?

choices.text: The token was forged with a copy of the CI's key
choices.why: Nothing was forged. The CI server signed it, as it signs one for every branch.

choices.text: `bound_issuer` was missing from the method's configuration
choices.why: It was set, and the token's issuer matched it.

choices.text: A dev-mode Vault accepts any token presented
choices.why: The same server refused three tokens a minute later.

choices.text: The role never looked at which branch the token named
choices.why: Right. The CI signs a valid token for every branch, and a role that trusts the signature alone trusts all of them.

prompt: Put the steps of a run of `main` reading the signing password through `ci/vault-read.sh` in order.
items: the CI server mints a token for `refs/heads/main`
the script logs in to `auth/jwt/login` with role and token
Vault answers with a token carrying `linkbox-sign`

prompt: Why does `ci/vault-read.sh` read the field with `jq -e`?

choices.text: So the password never appears in the run's log
choices.why: `jq -e` prints the value like plain `jq`; what it changes is the exit status.

choices.text: So a refused read fails the stage loudly
choices.why: Right. Instead of passing on an empty password, a missing field is an error, so the script fails closed with Vault's message.

choices.text: To decode the base64 in Vault's answer
choices.why: Vault answers plain JSON; nothing in it is base64.

choices.text: To strip the newline that `cmp` would see
choices.why: `-e` is about the exit status, and the comparison said `same`.

prompt: The `main` token logged in twice within its five minutes and Vault accepted both. If that token leaked into a log, what limits the damage?

choices.text: Vault refuses a token whose `jti` it has seen
choices.why: The capture shows the opposite: the same token logged in twice.

choices.text: The `trap` revokes it when the script ends
choices.why: The `trap` revokes the Vault token. The identity token is a JWT nobody can revoke.

choices.text: Its audience and its life: it is good at Vault only, until `exp`
choices.why: Right. Within that window it works for whoever holds it, which is why logs must not print it.

choices.text: Its signature changes after the first use
choices.why: A signature is fixed when the token is minted.

prompt: Which of these logins did the lesson's Vault refuse? Choose every one.

choices.text: a token minted for the audience `registry`
choices.why: Refused: invalid audience.

choices.text: a `try-something` token at the role `linkbox-any`
choices.why: Accepted, which was the defect the bound role fixed.

choices.text: a token signed by a key Vault had never seen
choices.why: Refused: no known key validated the signature.

choices.text: the `main` token used a second time
choices.why: Accepted: a JWT works for whoever holds it until it expires.

choices.text: a `try-something` token at the role `linkbox-main`
choices.why: Refused: the `ref` claim did not match.

prompt: An AWS role trusts GitHub's token service with a condition on `aud` and none on `sub`. Whose workflows can assume it?

choices.text: Every repository that asks for that audience
choices.why: Right. GitHub's issuer signs for every repository, so any of them that asks for that audience gets in.

choices.text: Those of the repository that registered the provider
choices.why: The provider is registered for the account, and it is the same issuer for everybody.

choices.text: No workflow, since AWS rejects a role without `sub`
choices.why: The policy is valid as written. That is why it is a mistake people ship.

choices.text: Those of the account owner's own organisation
choices.why: Nothing in an `aud` condition names an organisation.

prompt: A deploy role requires `sub` = `repo:ana/linkbox:ref:refs/heads/main`. The team adds `environment: production` to the deploy job, and the job can no longer assume the role. Why?

choices.text: An environment requires `id-token: read` instead of `write`
choices.why: There is no such variant; the permission is the same with or without an environment.

choices.text: The job's subject becomes the environment form, with no `ref`
choices.why: Right. Bind the role to `environment:production` and let the environment's rules choose branches.

choices.text: Environments remove the `aud` claim from the token
choices.why: The audience is whatever the job asks for, environment or not.

choices.text: Protection rules hold every token until a person approves
choices.why: Approval gates the job's start; once it runs, its token carries the environment subject.

prompt: Configured with `___` instead of a pasted public key, Vault fetches the issuer's published keys and follows a rotation on its own.
Match each question of minimal scope to what answered it in this lesson.

pairs.right: a policy naming one path with `read`

right_distractors: masking the value in the run's log

prompt: Which change removes the long-lived credential from linkbox's pipeline, instead of moving it somewhere else?

choices.text: Moving the password from `~/ci/keys` into Vault
choices.why: Then the run needs a Vault token, which is the same problem one step on.

choices.text: Keeping a Vault token in the hook's environment for every run
choices.why: That token is long-lived and readable by every run: the password with a new name.

choices.text: A token the CI signs per run, checked by Vault
choices.why: Right. The run holds nothing durable; it presents a statement that dies in five minutes.

choices.text: Encrypting the password file with a second key
choices.why: The second key is now the long-lived secret the run needs.
